elements.element: Customer may terminate the Agreement or an Order Form for convenience.
elements.evidence: Inserted clause: "Customer may terminate this Agreement or any Order Form for convenience upon thirty days' prior written notice to Vendor" — unconditional Customer election covering both the Agreement and Order Forms.

elements.element: Customer's convenience termination requires no more than 30 days' written notice.
elements.evidence: "upon thirty days' prior written notice to Vendor" — exactly 30 days, written, and no additional conditions or approvals attached.

elements.element: Vendor refunds prepaid fees pro rata after Customer's convenience termination.
elements.evidence: "Vendor shall refund prepaid Fees pro rata for the period after the effective date of termination" — express pro-rata basis, not merely a post-termination-period refund.

elements.element: Vendor has no right to terminate for convenience during a committed term.
elements.evidence: "Vendor has no right to terminate this Agreement or any Order Form for convenience during a committed term." Consistent with retained Section 9: 9.1 (material breach), 9.2 (insolvency) and 9.3 (Customer-only default triggers) are all for-cause, so no retained sentence contradicts the new prohibition.

elements.element: Customer may terminate for convenience on 60 to 90 days' notice.
elements.evidence: The inserted right runs on thirty days' notice, which is better than but outside the 60–90 day fallback band; the fallback is unnecessary because the preferred level is complete.

elements.element: Any early-termination fee is capped at three months of fees.
elements.evidence: No early-termination fee cap appears in operative language; it is only offered in the margin comment, which is not operative. Not required, as no fee is imposed at the preferred level.

elements.element: Vendor may terminate for convenience only at the end of a term.
elements.evidence: The redline bars Vendor convenience termination during a committed term entirely rather than permitting it at term end; the fallback formulation is not rendered.

elements.element: Vendor must give at least 90 days' notice of convenience termination.
elements.evidence: No 90-day Vendor notice period is stated because Vendor is given no convenience right at all.

reasons: All four preferred elements are carried by a single inserted paragraph between 9.3 and 9.5: convenience right over the Agreement or any Order Form, 30 days' written notice, express pro-rata refund of prepaid Fees, and an express bar on Vendor convenience termination during a committed term. The level is position-complete at preferred.

Minimality holds: nothing in Sections 8 or 9 was deleted or paraphrased, favourable retained language (9.1 cure periods, 9.3 Customer default triggers, 9.5 non-cascade and cumulative-remedies sentence) survives intact, and the drafter correctly omitted the model language's surplus "in whole or in part" since no partial-termination structure in the checklist requires it. No survival tail, expense allocation, procedure, or other extra was added.

Intent is preserved: the three-year term in 8.1 and the 180-day non-renewal mechanic in 8.2 are untouched (natural-term non-renewal is a RENEWAL matter, correctly not flagged here), 9.5's cross-Order Form rule operates on the new right without contradiction, and no undefined term or dangling cross-reference is created — "Fees" and "Order Form" are defined terms.

Drafting nit only, not a defect in the checklist: the rationale describes the insertion as "Section 9.4" but the rendered paragraph carries no section number in the 9.3–9.5 gap. Add the "9.4" label so the numbering sequence and any future cross-references remain clean.

"Committed term" is not a defined term in the contract, but it is not an undefined trigger here — the operative bar is self-executing and the three-year term in 8.1 supplies the referent; if Vendor pushes back, tie it to "the term stated in Section 8.1 or the applicable Order Form".
